rv.q: You don't need a worrying weakness for whimsy to enjoy this piece.
Rylance's play continually risks hippy whimsy. It pulls off something better.

If it is really true that there are some actors you would come to hear read the phone book, Rylance is one of them. Here he has indulged a personal passion for the prose poetry of Louis Jenkins to fashion a tapestry out of the writer’s work that functions as a kind of weird meditation on life itself.
He is a very unusual man, but he is undoubtedly a brilliant one.

It all depends on what you want from an evening in the theatre. If you are happy to watch Mark Rylance playing an eccentric loner who feels love and life have passed him by, this may be enough. Personally, I hunger for something more substantial.

Those coming to him afresh may want to sit this one out and wait for the resurfacing of his game-changing glory – Johnny Byron in Jez Butterworth’s Jerusalem, a part he has said he’d love to tackle again.
Ultimately, though, they say nothing more than 'Gee, life's a funny old thing', and the whole brief evening is about as enlightening as Billy the bigmouthed bass crooning 'Don't Worry, Be Happy'.

It is unorthodox, inherently philosophical and blissfully performed, and I would recommend anyone with a whimsical yet dark sense of humour to grab a seat.
This undemanding and under-written frivolity may bring complaints that he's got his priorities mixed up. Instead of entertaining us he's just entertaining himself.

The opening scenes in which the men trade anecdotes, as though two of Samuel Beckett’s tramps had been transported into a bucolic Coen brothers’comedy, exude a certain whimsical charm. But the play rapidly descends into hollow absurdism. Finally, in desperation, Rylance throws character and credibility to the wind.
